source.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Bart Bussmann; Noa Nabeshima; Adam Karvonen; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature absorption, splitting, and learned-feature geometry using a synthetic hierarchical dataset and SAE evaluations on language-model activations, rather than reproducing the original superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports reconstruction, downstream language-model loss, automated interpretability, and board-game results; these do not directly measure the listed claim versions. Background claims attributed to other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a methods paper (Matryoshka SAEs vs other SAEs). Its baseline measurements still bear on V5. With standard SAEs, a general latent develops holes as the dictionary grows, first-letter absorption is 0.49, and toy SAEs fail to recover ground-truth features. A change of training objective largely removes these failures. So which SAE features you get depends on dictionary size and objective, which bears on whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical. V1 is not tested: the toy model has 20 features in 20 dimensions and studies hierarchy, not superposition. V4 is assumed rather than tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also argue that absorption and splitting are artifacts of myopic training objectives, not fundamental limits of SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse autoencoders, including on a synthetic hierarchical-feature dataset and on language-model activations, and compares training objectives and SAE architectures. It does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method or its sparsity and feature-to-dimension sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE architecture and training objective change the reported feature absorption, splitting, and geometry. The paper also reports differences across dictionary sizes and sparsity levels.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE feature composition: decoder max cosine similarity is lower for Matryoshka SAEs, and meta-SAEs explain 55% vs 42% of decoder variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAE latents are compositions of more basic latents, and the amount of composition depends on the training objective.

record.problems: Several results relevant to SAE feature quality are qualitative or reported only as text descriptions of figures, without numerical scores or uncertainty estimates. The toy experiment does not report a feature-to-dimension or sparsity sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Reconstruction and downstream cross-entropy comparisons, automated interpretability scores, board-game metrics, and results about ablation variants were omitted because they do not directly measure the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: Not tested at all. The toy model has 20 features in d=20, with no sparsity sweep, no superposition transition and no geometry analysis.
Assumed, not tested. The paper does not measure how features spread across neurons, or whether SAEs recover sparse features beyond comparisons between methods.
The paper does not directly test whether features are canonical across random seeds.

missing.what: Meta-SAEs explain 55% of variance in BatchTopK decoder directions vs 42% for Matryoshka, and the gap grows with dictionary size. This is evidence that standard SAE latents are not atomic units.
As dictionary size grows (4k, 16k, 65k), other architectures often degrade on downstream metrics while Matryoshka SAEs improve or stay stable.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's links to V1 and V4 were wrong. The toy model is about hierarchical absorption with features no more numerous than dimensions, and the Gemma results are method benchmarks. Most Gemma rows are comparisons of the study's own method with others. The V5 bearing comes from the baseline SAE pathologies and their dependence on the training objective.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report a sweep over feature sparsity or the number of features relative to dimensions, nor a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometric phase. Its toy experiment concerns hierarchical feature absorption.
The study measures SAE feature absorption and splitting, not polysemanticity of network neurons, feature importance, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test causes of polysemantic neurons independent of capacity pressure.
The study evaluates SAE features on TinyStories and Gemma-2-2B activations, but does not measure how features are distributed across neurons.
The study does not establish whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of a model’s representation.
The study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: synthetic hierarchical feature model
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned decoder vectors with ground-truth feature vectors using cosine similarity
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between learned decoder vectors and ground-truth feature vectors
rows.value: High similarity between parent and child latents; the authors describe redundant representations and failure to disentangle hierarchical features.
rows.note: The result concerns hierarchical feature absorption in a synthetic setting; it does not establish a superposition transition or near-orthogonal geometry.
rows.check: Not V1: the toy has no more features than dimensions and no sparsity sweep. It bears on V5: a vanilla SAE fails to recover ground-truth hierarchical features (parent and child latents are highly similar).

rows.subject: synthetic hierarchical feature model
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned decoder vectors with ground-truth feature vectors using cosine similarity
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between learned decoder vectors and ground-truth feature vectors
rows.value: A clear diagonal similarity pattern; the learned vectors recover the true feature vectors with minimal overlap and only small nonzero off-diagonal terms.
rows.note: The reported geometry is qualitative and specific to this hierarchical toy setup.
rows.check: Not V1. It bears on V5 only as a contrast: with the Matryoshka objective, ground-truth features are recovered (diagonal similarity matrix), on a toy with a planted hierarchy.

rows.subject: 4-layer Transformer trained on TinyStories
rows.operation_detail: Inspected whether a general female-words latent retained activation on a specialized token
rows.measure: Coverage of the general female-words feature
rows.baseline: 300-latent reference SAE feature S/2/65 fires on female-coded tokens including Lily
rows.value: The corresponding 1000-latent general feature S/3/66 stops firing on Lily; the authors report that a Lily-specific latent S/3/359 absorbed that case.
rows.note: A qualitative example of SAE feature absorption across dictionary sizes.
rows.check: Relink from V4 to V5. The finding is that the general latent of the 300-latent SAE loses coverage of 'Lily' in the 1000-latent SAE, so SAE features are not stable across dictionary sizes. Qualitative, single example.

source_check.correct: state=partial: the general female-words latent retains a representation with systematic coverage holes; it stops firing on Lily when a specialized latent absorbs that case.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Female tokens absorption example; Figure 4.
source_check.problem: The general feature is incompletely represented, rather than wholly absent.

rows.subject: 4-layer Transformer trained on TinyStories
rows.operation_detail: Inspected broad female-coded token coverage while specialized child latents were present

conditions.value: same average sparsity as the comparison

rows.baseline: The paper contrasts this with holes in the larger reference SAE’s general female-words feature.
rows.value: The Matryoshka SAE maintains broad coverage of female-coded tokens while also developing specialized child latents, including Sue, Lily, and female-names features without holes.
rows.note: The report is a qualitative inspection, not a quantified recovery rate.
rows.check: Relink from V4. A 25k Matryoshka SAE keeps broad coverage; this shows the features depend on the training objective. Qualitative, with no rate given.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, paragraph describing the 25k-latent Matryoshka SAE.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured absorption of first-letter features using probes on raw activations and corresponding SAE latents
rows.note: The paper reports this as preserving general first-letter features in the presence of specialized latents.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with a baseline. For V5, the useful fact is that the standard BatchTopK SAE absorption rate is 0.49 at L0=40, versus 0.05 for Matryoshka. Features are incomplete under the standard objective.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, Feature Absorption and Splitting; Figure 6.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured how many SAE latents were needed to capture first-letter classification information
rows.measure: Number of latents needed per first-letter feature
rows.baseline: BatchTopK SAE: three latents per first-letter feature
rows.value: Matryoshka SAE: one latent per first-letter feature on average
rows.note: The paper interprets this as reduced feature splitting.
rows.check: Method comparison. BatchTopK splits each first-letter feature over about 3 latents, Matryoshka over about 1, so the units depend on the objective.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, Feature Absorption and Splitting; Figure 6.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Encoded inputs with the SAE, mean-pooled non-padding tokens, selected the most relevant latent, and trained logistic-regression probes

conditions.value: 35 binary classification tasks across professions, sentiment, language, code, and news

rows.value: Best performance at lower sparsity levels; consistently outperforms standard BatchTopK SAEs across all sparsity levels.
rows.note: The paper gives no numeric values for these comparisons in the text.
rows.check: Benchmark comparison of the study's own method against other SAEs; no measure of the claim itself.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated latents encoding spurious signals and assessed classifier accuracy
rows.value: Matryoshka SAEs significantly outperform all benchmark architectures on SCR.
rows.note: No numeric scores are stated in the text.
rows.check: SCR benchmark comparing the study's own method with other architectures; no numbers in the text.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated latents specific to one class and measured effects on classifiers for that and other classes
rows.value: Matryoshka SAEs significantly outperform all benchmark architectures on TPP.
rows.note: No numeric scores are stated in the text.
rows.check: TPP benchmark comparing the study's own method with other architectures; no numbers in the text.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared each decoder vector’s maximum cosine similarity to another latent’s decoder vector
rows.measure: Average maximum cosine similarity between decoder vectors
rows.value: Substantially lower for Matryoshka SAEs; the paper interprets this as less feature composition.
rows.note: The text does not state the numerical cosine values.
rows.check: Decoder cosine similarity as a proxy for composition, comparing the study's own method with others; no values in the text.

relationships.condition: Standard SAEs (vanilla toy SAE, TinyStories reference SAEs, BatchTopK on Gemma-2-2B layer 12)
relationships.reason: Standard SAEs miss ground-truth toy features (R1), develop holes as the dictionary grows (R3), show first-letter absorption of 0.49 and split each letter over about 3 latents (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Standard SAEs missed ground-truth toy features and developed holes as the dictionary grew; on Gemma-2-2B they showed first-letter absorption of 0.49 and split each letter over about 3 latents.

source_check.condition: Standard SAEs (vanilla toy SAE, TinyStories reference SAEs, BatchTopK on Gemma-2-2B layer 12)
source_check.reason: R1 reports failed hierarchical ground-truth recovery; R3 explicitly demonstrates lost coverage across dictionary sizes; R5 and R6 quantify absorption and splitting, contradicting complete, stable units in these settings.

relationships.condition: Matryoshka SAE objective vs standard objective
relationships.reason: Changing the training objective restores toy ground truth (R2) and broad coverage (R4), and cuts absorption to 0.05 (R5, R6). So the features recovered depend on the objective chosen, at a small reconstruction cost.
relationships.display_finding: Switching to the Matryoshka objective restored toy ground truth and broad coverage and cut absorption to 0.05, at a small reconstruction cost.

relation.reason: Its own synthetic and language-model measurements test the completeness and stability of recovered SAE features.

tranche.reason: The baseline results directly qualify V5 through failed ground-truth recovery, absorption and splitting; the objective comparison demonstrates dependence on training choices.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v1, dated 21 March 2025. Improved recovery and reduced absorption do not establish complete or canonical dictionaries; decoder cosine similarity and meta-SAE variance are composition proxies.

statements.correction: Appendix D.1, largest dictionary: meta-SAEs explain 55% of BatchTopK decoder-direction variance and 42% of Matryoshka decoder-direction variance. Section 4.3, Figure 8: Matryoshka has lower average maximum decoder cosine similarity.
statements.problem: The meta-SAE variance percentages are assigned to the opposite architectures. The lower decoder cosine similarity claim is correct.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The toy results show that learned-direction similarity and absorption differ by SAE training method, but do not test the claimed sparsity-dependent superposition regime (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports recovered or useful SAE features in language-model activations, alongside measured absorption, splitting, probing, and concept-isolation outcomes (R3–R10).
